title: Some Christians Want Heaven Without Surrendering Their Lives to Christ
paragraphs: Some Christians Want Heaven Without Surrendering Their Lives to Christ
We want Jesus to save us from hell. But what happens when we don’t want Him to rule the life He saved?
There is a version of Christianity that almost everyone can tolerate.
Jesus takes you to heaven when you die.
But then Jesus says something that suddenly makes the room uncomfortable:
Not fit Me into the parts of your life where I cause the least inconvenience.
And that is where Christianity stops being merely comforting and becomes costly.
Because many people want the destination Jesus promises while resisting the surrender Jesus commands.
but we still want ownership of ourselves.
A cross that removes our guilt without a cross that confronts our rebellion.
We want Jesus close enough to rescue us, but sometimes not close enough to rearrange us.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that someone openly rejects Christ.
Perhaps it is that someone can spend years around Christian language, Christian music, Christian churches, Christian posts, Christian friends, and Christian activities...
and still quietly resist giving Christ the throne.
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
The Greek is even more arresting:
Εἴ τις θέλει ὀπίσω μου ἔρχεσθαι, ἀρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν καὶ ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καθ’ ἡμέραν καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι.
Ei tis thelei opisō mou erchesthai, arnēsasthō heauton kai aratō ton stauron autou kath’ hēmeran kai akoloutheitō moi.
The verb ἀρνησάσθω — arnēsasthō carries the force of denying or disowning.
Jesus was not calling His disciples to hate themselves.
He was confronting something much deeper:
the human insistence on being our own final authority.
We naturally want to belong to Jesus while remaining sovereign over ourselves.
We want Him to forgive our past while asking permission before touching our future.
Then He reaches toward our relationships...
and suddenly our hands tighten around the very things we said belonged to Him.
And sometimes we discover that the thing we cannot imagine surrendering has quietly become the thing we are serving.
Because surrender becomes real precisely where obedience begins to cost us something.
There is a young man in the Gospels who discovered this.
From the outside, this looks like the dream encounter.
And Mark tells us something beautiful that we must never overlook:
And because Jesus loved him, Jesus did not flatter him.
Christ touched the place where surrender had not yet happened.
For this particular man, his possessions had become spiritually decisive. Jesus commanded him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences in Scripture:

“Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.”
—Mark 10:22
He came asking about eternal life...
and walked away because surrender cost more than he expected.
Do not turn that passage into the simplistic claim that every Christian must sell every possession. Scripture does not teach that.
The knife cuts deeper than that.
Jesus exposed the rival master in this man's heart.
What would Jesus touch in your life that could make you walk away sorrowful?
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows about.
Maybe it is bitterness you have baptized as “boundaries.”
Maybe you need everyone to think you are spiritually strong.
Maybe it is the secret conversation you keep deleting.
Maybe it is an addiction you keep promising God you will surrender “eventually.”
Maybe it is simply the right to tell Jesus:
The room inside the heart where we have hung a sign:
JESUS, YOU MAY ENTER EVERYWHERE EXCEPT HERE.
Still tell people we are Christians.
And perhaps nobody suspects that behind that locked door something is slowly suffocating our fellowship with Christ.
This is why Jesus' words in Matthew 7 are so sobering.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven...”
—Matthew 7:21
But calling Jesus Lord and submitting to Jesus as Lord are not identical things.
This does not mean Christians earn salvation by achieving flawless obedience.
If that were the Gospel, none of us could stand.

“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works...”
—Ephesians 2:8–9
Not performing our way into heaven.
But do not stop reading before verse 10.
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works...”
We are not saved by good works.
But saving grace does not leave us peacefully married to rebellion.
Grace does not merely change our destination.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
The same grace that forgives you also trains you.
The grace that receives you also transforms you.
The grace that washes you does not lovingly leave you lying in the mud.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is one of grace's beautiful consequences.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning that reorients a person toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling terrible about what you did.
People can cry because sin hurt them without actually turning from the sin that owns them.
I don't want to keep defending what nailed You to the cross.
And sometimes those words come through tears.
Sometimes they come from someone sitting alone at 2:17 in the morning staring at a phone screen and realizing...
“I have become someone I never thought I would become.”
You promised God this would be the last time.
That voice wants you running away from Christ precisely when you desperately need to run toward Him.
“Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”
Hours later, fear dismantled his confidence.
Three times Peter denied knowing Christ.
Luke records a detail that feels almost unbearable:

“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
—Luke 22:61
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
The man who said he would die with Jesus could not even admit knowing Him.
If Peter's story ended there, many of us would understand it.
Because we know what it feels like to disappoint ourselves.
We know what it feels like to whisper:
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to tell Peter that repentance was unnecessary.
Peter's scandal was not the final sentence.
But grace did not restore Peter so Peter could return to the courtyard and keep denying Christ.
Grace restored him to follow Christ.
Jesus does not merely forgive the person you were.
He begins remaking the person you are becoming.
This is why surrender is not God trying to steal your life.

“For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.”
—Luke 9:24
The great paradox of Christianity is that the life we desperately try to preserve apart from Christ is the very life we lose.
And when we surrender ourselves to Christ, we discover that He was never trying to destroy us.
He was rescuing us from the false gods that were destroying us.
Then trains you to consume people.
Then chains you to the person who hurt you.
Then makes you terrified of rejection.
Then makes every uncontrollable moment unbearable.
Not merely a ticket to heaven.
And Christianity makes no sense without Him at the center.

“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”
—Galatians 2:20
That is stronger than adding Jesus to your existing identity.
The Gospel is death and resurrection.
Sanctification is not instant sinless perfection.

“If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves...”
—1 John 1:8

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
So this article is not asking:
It is asking something far more searching:
When Christ confronts you, do you keep running toward Him or are you constructing a Christianity that allows you to keep running from Him?
There is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and deciding you no longer want to get up.
There is a difference between weakness that cries for mercy and rebellion that demands God stop calling it sin.
Not because condemnation is the goal.
Because freedom begins where hiding ends.
You do not need to impress Jesus today.
You need to come into the light.
Bring Him the secret browser history.
Bring Him the part of yourself you are ashamed to name.
Bring Him even your resistance to surrender.
You may have arrived at this article thinking your greatest need was to try harder.
Powerful enough to forgive what you cannot undo.
Powerful enough to break what you cannot defeat alone.
Powerful enough to resurrect what sin has buried.
The cross destroys both our pride and our despair.
It destroys pride because our sin was so serious that Christ had to die.
It destroys despair because His love was so great that Christ willingly did.
That is why your scandal does not have to become your identity.
The ashamed can step into the light.
Not because sin suddenly became insignificant...
but because Jesus is a greater Savior than we dared imagine.
So stop negotiating with the One who was crucified for you.
Stop offering Jesus visitation rights to a life He purchased with His blood.
Stop saying “someday” to obedience when tomorrow was never promised.
If there is something you need to confess, confess it.
If there is someone you need to forgive, begin.
If there is a sinful relationship you need to leave, seek godly help and obey Christ.
If addiction has become stronger than your private resolutions, bring trustworthy believers into the battle.
If you have wandered from fellowship, come home.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ...
Not when you've repaired your reputation.
Not after you've made yourself worthy.
Come because sinners are exactly the people Christ came to save.
And if you're reading this with tears because you know exactly which locked room Christ has been touching...
you don't have to describe everything publicly.
But don't hide from Him anymore.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Christ still restores broken people.
The friend whose faith is fading.
The brother who keeps pretending everything is fine.
The husband nobody knows is struggling.
The believer who has learned Christian vocabulary while slowly losing intimacy with Christ.
Or send this privately if their struggle is too personal for a public tag.
Not because an article is sacred, but because there may come a night when you need to remember that surrender is not the doorway into losing Christ.
It is what following Christ looks like.
Not as a performance of spirituality, and never because sharing a post earns favor with God.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can also be an act of voluntary generosity and partnership when it flows from love rather than pressure. Scripture teaches cheerful, willing giving—not purchasing God's favor.

Following Gospel Warrior helps you stay connected to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen—to follow along.
Christ already told us what glorifies the Father: lives bearing fruit as His disciples.
And in Christ, failure does not have to write your final chapter either.
Maybe heaven was what first made you look toward Jesus.
But Jesus Himself is the treasure.
And one day, when every possession is gone, every applause has faded, every temptation has finally fallen silent, and everything you once fought desperately to keep has slipped from your hands...
You were never surrendering your life to Someone trying to take it from you.
You were surrendering it to the One who gave His life to bring you home.
The hands asking you to surrender are still marked by the nails that prove how far He went to save you.
